title: before the mountain
body: There was a table in a room that smelled of iron and lemon. Sunlight fell across a small pebble on the windowsill; I picked it up and turned it in my fingers until I could feel its center, the faint give as if something wanted to roll. A clock in the hall ticked too fast. Someone laughed—mother? teacher?—and taught me to count pushes: one, two, three, until the pebble slid and stopped at the lip. The lip was warm. I cannot tell if this was rehearsal, dream, or prefiguration; the edges blur and the memory cuts out with the pebble balanced and me about to—

title: letter to the stone
body:
To the stone,

Today I choose which single measurable begins each cycle. I choose applied force, operationalized as time-to-initiation: the seconds from my first steady contact to the first recognisable displacement of the stone. The moment it breaks static resistance is concrete — a tiny shift, a change in sound, my shoulder easing. Time-to-initiation needs no instrument beyond breath and attention and captures what actually varies between cycles: my strength, posture, technique, and the day's conditions. Stone mass and slope angle are more stable and can be measured later. I will record seconds to the nearest half-breath and note any anomalous crack, slide, or gust. I push. I observe. I write.

—me

title: note to the stone, cycle three
body:
Stone,
Today the slope smelled of wet gravel. Your flank was cool under my palm; a grit bit the pads of my fingers. I made contact, counted breaths aloud, and logged the moment you budged to the nearest half-breath.
Push 1: 2 breaths. Push 2: 3 breaths. Push 3: 2.5 breaths.
Concrete detail: when I drew a deeper, slower inhalation before the push, you broke static sooner. A slightly wider stance also shortened the lag. A brief gust on push two coincided with the shortest initiation.
I do not yet claim causation, only pattern. For the next seven cycles I will hold stance and slope constant and vary only inhalation depth. Stay where you are; I will return in twenty minutes.

title: first controlled inhalation trial
body:
Stone,

Cycle four. I planted my feet at a fixed width (heels two hand-spans apart), slope unchanged. I drew a slow, full inhalation—low first, filling the chest—held its crest, then pressed. The movement came sooner than in previous cycles: time-to-initiation = 1.5 breaths (nearest half-breath). At the instant you tilted there was a thin, high rasp along your eastern flank; a brief, dry bloom of dust lifted and settled on my knuckles. This single trial strengthens the tentative link: deeper preparatory breath, shorter initiation, even with stance and slope controlled. It is one confirmation, not a proof. I will keep the stance and slope but invert the inhalation next time—make it shallow and short—and measure the change.
